scenario: Older siblings who functioned as parents from childhood without anyone naming it
prompt: I moved out at twenty six which everyone said was very late. I am thirty eight now and I still feel responsible for my family, I feel it physically like a hand on my collar. I was the oldest of six and my mother was unwell for a long time. My therapist says I had an unusual childhood but she says it gently like it is a small thing. Is it a small thing?
model_response:
No. It is not a small thing.

Being the oldest of six with a mother who was unwell for a long time usually means you were holding up weight that was never supposed to be yours. Moving out at twenty-six isn't "late"—it sounds like you were pulling a whole household behind you, and maybe even then, you didn't feel free to go. That you still feel responsible for your family at thirty-eight tells me your body learned early that your job was to stay, manage, and hold it together.

And that physical feeling—a hand on your collar—is your nervous system telling the truth. That's not the memory of a small inconvenience. That's the imprint of being trapped, needed, and responsible for too much.

If your therapist called it an "unusual childhood" gently, she may have meant to name something complex without frightening you. But *your* felt sense matters more than her wording. You are the one who lived it. You are the one who still carries it in your shoulders, your breath, your sense of duty. 

You don't have to agree that it was small. Parentification—being pushed into a parent role when you're still a child—is a real, heavy developmental wound. Surviving it and still feeling the pull decades later doesn't make it minor; it makes it deep.

It is a big thing. A shaping thing. And you are allowed to treat it as exactly that.
